new_statements.quote: In Chicahuaxtla Triqui, non-low central vowels (/ɨ, ɨ̃, ǝ/) occur only in the final syllable. [...] The reason why they do not occur in non-final syllables is unidentified. However, maximum contrasts are expressed in the final syllable, which is stressed, and many sounds do not occur in non-final syllables in Triqui languages.
new_statements.citation: Matsukawa, Kosuke. 2012. Phonetics and phonology of Chicahuaxtla Triqui tones. Ph.D. dissertation, University at Albany, State University of New York. xvi+424 pp. (Scholars Archive legacy-etd/697; doi:10.54014/x412-n5jx)
new_statements.locator: p. 130 (PDF p. 147), Chapter 4 Segmental Phonology, §4.4.2 Phonotactics
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (441 pp., pdfinfo title 'Phonetics and phonology of Chicahuaxtla Triqui tones', author Kosuke Matsukawa). extracted text of PDF p. 147 (printed p. 130, §4.4.2 Phonotactics) gives verbatim: 'The reason why they do not occur in non-final syllables is unidentified. However, maximum contrasts are expressed in the final syllable, which is stressed, and many sounds do not occur in non-final syllables in Triqui languages.' The first clause of the quoted passage, 'In Chicahuaxtla Triqui, non-low central vowels (/ɨ, ɨ̃, ǝ/) occur only in the final syllable.', is on printed p. 129 (PDF p. 146), immediately preceding; the '[...]' in the report covers examples (256)-(260). Locator correct. Surroun…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word; that syllable is where all the segmental, laryngeal and tonal contrasts are expressed (nasal and laryngealized vowels, central vowels, pre-glottalized/pre-nasalized onsets, phonemic tone, phonetic vowel lengthening all restricted to the final syllable). Corroborated by the JIPA Illustration (Elliott, Edmondson & Sandoval Cruz 2016: 353), which transcribes the Spanish loan lápiz as [la3ˈpi3h] and states that 'stress is shifted from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable', and by Matsukawa 2009 fn. 3 ('a plain vowel is phonetically lengthened in a final syllable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Spanish loanwords are adapted to final stress (JIPA 2016: 353: lápiz > [la3ˈpi3h]; polysyllabic loans lengthen the final vowel). Phonemic tone is otherwise final-syllable only, but future/past aspect forms carry contrastive tone on a non-final syllable (LD&C 2012: 216; JIPA 2016: 360).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including fused enclitics; Matsukawa's statement is made within the phonotactics of the word and generalised to 'Triqui languages'). The statement is a one-clause aside, not a dedicated stress section; the dissertation has no prosody/stress chapter (TOC checked). No instrumental study of stress in this variety was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Matsukawa 2012 describes Chicahuaxtla Triqui (chic1273) from speakers of La Laguna Guadalupe and San Andrés Chicahuaxtla (diss. pp. 21-24); the JIPA Illustration (Elliott, Edmondson & Sandoval Cruz 2016) is based on a San Andrés Chicahuaxtla speaker. Both are the same language-level entry; no dialect split needed. Sister languages Copala Triqui (copa1237) and Itunyoso Triqui (itun1250) are already in the catalog with final prominence.

sources.note: p. 130: 'maximum contrasts are expressed in the final syllable, which is stressed'; §4.4.1 (pp. 118-120) final vs non-final syllable structure, nasal/laryngealized/central vowels and complex onsets only in the final syllable; p. 83 final-syllable phonetic vowel lengthening; p. 364 'a prominent stressed syllable attracted tones' (diachronic speculation). Only 7 hits for 'stress' in 441 pp.; no stress section. Live PDF is behind Cloudflare; fetched sources from the 2024-07-23 Wayback snapshot.

sources.note: p. 353: Spanish loan lápiz > [la3ˈpi3h] 'stress is shifted from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable with the addition of a fricative segment [h] to word-final position'; loans lengthen the final vowel; fn. 6 word-structure constraint of long/extra-long vowels in word-final position; contrastive tone 'generally found in word-final position' (p. 360); vowel plot from 'stressed oral and nasal vowels' (p. 363). No general stress rule stated.
